title: RFC 8785 Section 3.1 — input data constraints (DERIVED)
$comment: DERIVED — not verbatim. RFC 8785 ships NO JSON Schema, NO CDDL and NO ABNF of its own; its only formal artifact is the ECMAScript sample canonicalizer of Appendix A, held verbatim in this directory as canonicalizer.ecmascript.js. Every keyword in this file was written for this record and MUST NOT be quoted as RFC 8785's own schema. ||| DERIVED FROM: RFC 8785, 'JSON Canonicalization Scheme (JCS)', Rundgren/Jordan/Erdtman, June 2020, Independent Submission, <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8785.txt> — Section 3.1 'Creation of Input Data' in full, with its Note on Unicode Normalization; Section 3.2.2.3 (NaN/Infinity); Appendix D 'Dealing with Big Numbers'; Appendix E 'String Subtype Handling'. The I-JSON subset itself is RFC 7493, which Section 3.1 incorporates by reference and which this record does not hold. ||| SCOPE: this schema constrains the INPUT to canonicalization — the data a producer is about to canonicalize. It does NOT describe JCS OUTPUT; that is canonical-output.abnf. The two are different languages: every JCS output is also valid JCS input, but almost no JCS input is already canonical. ||| HONESTY NOTE: three of Section 3.1's four constraints are only PARTLY expressible in JSON Schema and one is not expressible at all. Each gap is recorded in the relevant $comment below and collected under $defs/NOT-EXPRESSIBLE. Nothing here is faked with an approximation that would silently pass non-conforming data.

i-json-value.$comment: RFC 8785 Section 3.1 applies to the whole input tree. RFC 8259 permits any JSON value at the top level and RFC 8785 does not narrow that, so this schema is rooted at a value rather than at an object. In practice a JCS producer canonicalizes an object, but nothing in the document requires it.

i-json-object.$comment: Section 3.1: 'JSON objects MUST NOT exhibit duplicate property names.' ||| NOT EXPRESSIBLE. JSON Schema has no duplicate-key keyword, and in the general case it cannot have one: the JSON Schema data model (2020-12, section 4.2.1) defines an object as an *unordered set of name/value pairs* in which 'the names in an object SHOULD be unique' — i.e. by the time a document has been parsed into the schema data model, duplicates have ALREADY been resolved, usually last-wins, and the evidence that there were two is gone. uniqueItems works on arrays only and there is no analogue for names. ||| This is the single most important constraint in Section 3.1 and this schema CANNOT CHECK IT. It is also unexpressible in canonical-output.abnf (see that file's gap item 2), so it is unexpressible in BOTH derived schema languages in this directory. ||| HOW TO ACTUALLY CHECK IT: a duplicate-name check must run on the raw token stream, before or during parsing — not on a parsed tree and not with this schema. Any harness that validates with this file alone has silently skipped a MUST.

i-json-array.$comment: RFC 8785 places no constraint on arrays beyond those on their elements. Section 3.2.3 requires that 'array element order MUST NOT be changed' during canonicalization, which is a constraint on the TRANSFORMATION, not on the input document, and so has no expression here. Appendix E.1 notes that because arrays may mix types, 'custom parsing and serialization code may be required to cope with subtypes anyway' — guidance, not a schema constraint.

i-json-string.$comment: Section 3.1: 'JSON string data MUST be expressible as Unicode [UNICODE].' Applies to property names too — Section 3.2.2.2 says 'JSON string data (which includes JSON object property names as well)'. ||| PARTLY EXPRESSIBLE. 'type: string' is as far as this goes, and it is weaker than it looks. The real content of the rule is Section 3.2.2.2's Note: 'invalid Unicode data like "lone surrogates" (e.g., U+DEAD) may lead to interoperability issues including broken signatures, [so] occurrences of such data MUST cause a compliant JCS implementation to terminate with an appropriate error.' A lone surrogate is exactly a string that is NOT expressible as Unicode. ||| WHY NO PATTERN IS SET HERE: a regex for lone surrogates is not portable across JSON Schema implementations. JSON Schema 2020-12 specifies ECMA-262 regular expressions but explicitly does NOT require the 'u' flag; without it, matching is over UTF-16 code units and '[\uD800-\uDBFF](?![\uDC00-\uDFFF])' works, while with it the same pattern behaves differently because the engine operates on code points. Worse, most validators are written in languages whose string type cannot hold a lone surrogate at all (Go, Rust, Python 3 str via the usual JSON parsers) — the parser has already substituted U+FFFD or raised, so the pattern would be testing a value that no longer carries the defect. A pattern that passes for the wrong reason is worse than a documented gap, so this field carries the finding instead. ||| HOW TO ACTUALLY CHECK IT: scan the raw input for an unpaired \uD800-\uDBFF escape and for an unpaired surrogate in the decoded text, before validation. Note that canonical-output.abnf CAN exclude lone surrogates structurally — see its lone-surrogate note — because an output grammar sees octets, which is a layer this schema does not reach. ||| ALSO NOT EXPRESSIBLE: the Section 3.1 Note — 'Although the Unicode standard offers the possibility of rearranging certain character sequences, referred to as "Unicode Normalization" [UCNORM], JCS-compliant string processing does not take this into consideration. That is, all components involved in a scheme depending on JCS MUST preserve Unicode string data "as is".' Both NFC-normalized and un-normalized forms of the same text are valid input; what is forbidden is a component CHANGING one into the other. That is a property of the pipeline, not of a document, so no schema over a single document can see it.

i-json-number.$comment: Section 3.1: 'JSON number data MUST be expressible as IEEE 754 [IEEE754] double-precision values.' ||| PARTLY EXPRESSIBLE. The minimum/maximum below bound the magnitude at the finite binary64 extremes, ±1.7976931348623157e+308 (Appendix B rows 7fefffffffffffff and ffefffffffffffff, 'Max pos number' / 'Max neg number'). That is a real check and it catches Appendix D's 'giantNumber': 1.4e+9999. ||| WHAT IS NOT EXPRESSIBLE, and it is the larger half: 'expressible as a double' means the decimal literal survives a decimal -> binary64 -> decimal round trip unchanged. JSON Schema has no such keyword and could not usefully have one, because by the time a validator applies 'minimum' the literal has usually ALREADY been parsed into a double and the round-trip damage has already happened and is invisible. Appendix D's 'int64Max': 9223372036854775807 is the canonical case: it is well inside the magnitude bounds this schema sets, so it VALIDATES — and it is not expressible as a double (it becomes 9223372036854775808). A validator that keeps arbitrary-precision numbers could in principle detect this; one that parses to double cannot, and the ones in common use parse to double. ||| Appendix B note (1) is adjacent but distinct, and is a SHOULD, not a MUST: 'For maximum compliance with the ECMAScript "JSON" object, values that are to be interpreted as true integers SHOULD be in the range -9007199254740991 to 9007199254740991. However, how numbers are used in applications does not affect the JCS algorithm.' That bound is deliberately NOT set below — it would reject input the MUST permits, and the sentence after it says the JCS algorithm is indifferent. A harness wanting the SHOULD should layer it separately. ||| NaN AND Infinity: Section 3.2.2.3 requires an implementation to terminate on them, and Appendix B note (3) says 'Values out of range are not permitted in JSON.' No constraint is needed or possible here — JSON has no syntax for NaN or Infinity, so a conforming JSON parser never produces one and a non-conforming extension (JSON5, Python's json with allow_nan) produces a token this schema's data model cannot represent. The requirement is real; its enforcement belongs to the parser, not to this file. ||| Appendix D's recommendation — 'numbers that do not have a natural place in the current JSON ecosystem MUST be wrapped using the JSON string type' and, in Section 3.1, 'it is RECOMMENDED to represent such numbers as JSON strings' — is a schema-DESIGN instruction to the author of an application schema, not a constraint on arbitrary input. An application schema derived from this one should type such fields as string; this file cannot know which fields those are.

i-json-literal.$comment: Section 3.2.2.1: 'In accordance with JSON [RFC8259], the literals "null", "true", and "false" MUST be serialized as null, true, and false, respectively.' That is an output rule; on the input side these three are simply the permitted non-string, non-number scalars. No constraint beyond the type.

NOT-EXPRESSIBLE.$comment: Collected findings — every RFC 8785 input-side rule this schema cannot enforce. Not a schema; never referenced. Listed here so the cross-check pass can reconcile against ../requirements.yaml without re-reading the $comments above. 1) Section 3.1 'JSON objects MUST NOT exhibit duplicate property names' — the JSON Schema data model has already collapsed duplicates; needs a raw-token check. 2) Section 3.1 / 3.2.2.2 Note, lone surrogates — unenforceable portably, and usually destroyed by the host parser before the validator runs. 3) Section 3.1 'MUST be expressible as IEEE 754 double-precision' — only the magnitude bound is expressible; the round-trip-exactness half is not, and 9223372036854775807 passes this schema while failing the requirement. 4) Section 3.1 'parsed JSON string data MUST NOT be altered during subsequent serializations', elaborated in Appendix E — a property of the pipeline, not of a document. Appendix E's own worked example, '055' becoming '55' and '2019-01-28T07:45:10Z' becoming '2019-01-28T07:45:10.000Z' under a reviver-based parse, produces data that validates perfectly against this schema and is exactly the failure Appendix E warns about. 5) Section 3.1 Note, Unicode normalization — likewise a pipeline property: the MUST is 'preserve as is', and both forms validate. 6) Section 3.2.2.3 / Appendix B note (3), NaN and Infinity — not representable in the data model; belongs to the parser. 7) Appendix B note (1), the ±9007199254740991 safe-integer range — a SHOULD, and deliberately not enforced because it is narrower than the MUST. 8) Appendix D / Section 3.1, wrapping big numbers as strings — a RECOMMENDED instruction to an application schema author, not checkable against arbitrary input. ||| Items 1, 4 and 5 are the dangerous ones: in each case non-conforming data validates CLEANLY, so a green result from this schema is not evidence that Section 3.1 was met.
